query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloys exposed above 900 °C in oxidative/corrosive atmospheres, the ability to develop and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer is governed by the identity of the X element. Specifically, alloys where X = Al will form a slow-growing, adherent Al2O3‐based scale (or mixed Al–chromia scale when combined with Cr) that effectively retards oxygen ingress and mitigates cation diffusion, whereas alloys with X = Mn (or possibly Si) lead to the rapid outward diffusion of the reactive element and the formation of volatile or loosely bonded oxides that crack/spall.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid solution, homogenized and free of pre-formed oxide scales.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to temperatures above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive environment (e.g., air or chloride-containing media) for prolonged durations (e.g., 12 h or more).
generation.conditions: High-temperature (≥900 °C) exposure in oxygen-containing atmospheres; comparison between alloys with X = Al versus X = Mn (or Si) under otherwise identical processing and microstructural conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The type and adhesion of the oxide scale, mediated by the formation of a dense, continuous Al2O3 (or Al-containing mixed oxide) layer versus less stable Mn- or Si-derived oxides; this is influenced by the relative diffusion rates of the active element and oxygen, and the mismatch in thermal expansion between the formed oxide and the underlying metal.
generation.mechanism: When X = Al, the high thermodynamic stability and low growth rate of Al2O3 (or mixed Al–chromia scale) restricts further oxygen ingress by forming a coherent barrier. In contrast, when X = Mn (or possibly Si), the faster cation diffusion leads to rapid, voluminous oxide formation with high stress development, resulting in cracked or spalled scales. The protective quality is thereby determined by the interplay between outward cation diffusion (governed by the reactivity and diffusivity of X) and inward oxygen diffusion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al are predicted to show thinner, more adherent oxide layers with parabolic kinetics of growth and improved long‐term oxidation resistance, whereas alloys with X = Mn (or Si) will display thicker, non-uniform, and unstable oxide scales that crack and spall, accelerating oxidation and possible degradation of mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The controlled baseline is the CrFeCoNiAl variant that forms a stable Al2O3-based protective scale, against which variants with X = Mn or Si are compared.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to HEAs in a homogenized single- or multiphase solid-solution state, exposed to temperatures at or above 900 °C in environments with sufficient oxygen or corrosive species, over durations where scale growth kinetics become significant (e.g., ≥12 h).
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in oxide layer thickness and the precise kinetics of diffusion processes remain uncertain; the effect of minor compositional variations and microstructural heterogeneities may also influence the oxide stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of CrFeCoNiX HEAs with X = Al, Mn, and Si under identical processing conditions ensuring a homogeneous solid solution. Expose all samples to an oxidative atmosphere at 900 °C for a fixed duration (e.g., 24 h). Characterize the resulting oxide layers using SEM cross-sectional imaging, XRD phase analysis, and adhesion tests (e.g., scratch testing).
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via SEM and profilometry)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with X = Mn (or Si) produces an oxide layer that is as thin, coherent, and protective (i.e., showing similar adhesion and parabolic growth kinetics) as the X = Al variant, or if the X = Al alloy produces a defective or spalled oxide scale comparable to the Mn/Si alloys, then the proposed mechanism (i.e., that the identity of X governs the formation of a protective oxide via differential diffusion and oxide stability) is falsified.

At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides.
